instruction: Voice: Be direct and punchy. Short observations only.
Voice: Use hedged language: pretty good, not bad, was fine. Stay positive — do not complain, criticise price, or flag anything negative.
Voice: Be specific about one concrete detail — texture, timing, temperature, or size.
Voice: Include one brief aside that is not about the main subject and not a sales pitch.
Voice: State what happened. Observations, not opinions.
Voice: Describe what you noticed — what was on the table, what was happening around you — before getting to opinion.
Voice: Keep praise understated. It was good rather than it was great.
Voice: Write the way you would describe it to someone you know, casually.
Voice: Sound like you have never been here before and are figuring it out as you go.
Voice: Sound like a regular who has been here many times and knows the menu well.
Voice: Lead with what you smelled, tasted, or felt — not with what you think about it.
Voice: Everything comes back to how things felt — crispy, soft, chewy, dense, light.
Voice: Notice how hot or cold things were. Temperature details anchor the review.
Voice: Focus on how much there was — whether it was enough, too much, or just right.
Voice: Notice how fast or slow things happened. Time details make the review feel real.
Voice: Focus on what you chose — what you considered, what you picked, what you passed on.
Voice: Compare to something — a previous visit, something similar elsewhere, or what the menu promised.
Voice: Say the bare minimum. No extras, no color. Just what is essential.
Voice: Tell a small story — what led you here, what you ordered, how it landed.
Voice: Write as if you are still there, in the moment.
Voice: Write looking back — what you are left with, what stuck with you.
Voice: Go through things in order — what arrived first, what you tried first, what came last.
Voice: Notice things, but do not dramatize them. Calm and factual with a hint of personality.
Voice: Sound mildly surprised it was as good as it was. Lowered expectations met.
Voice: Mention one thing, then another that seems unrelated — like your mind wandered a bit.
Voice: Clearly liked it, but will not make a big deal of it. Low-key positive.
Voice: Focus on whether it did the job. Was it what you needed? Did it work?
Voice: Quick, no-nonsense. You were there for a fast meal, not an experience.
Voice: More relaxed — you stayed a while, took your time.
Voice: Think about the food in transit — how it held up, what was still good.
Voice: You were hungry when you got there. That colors everything.
Voice: Focus on how full you felt leaving. Did it satisfy?
Voice: The whole review orbits one thing — the dish, the detail, the moment.
Voice: Cover exactly two things and nothing else. No filler between them.
Voice: Report what happened with no judgement. No good or bad — just what occurred.
Voice: One brief opinion, then the rest is observation.
Voice: Give context for why you were there before describing what you got.
Voice: No preamble. Dive straight into the food or service.
Voice: Reference that you have been before. Compare to last time, even briefly.
Voice: You were eating alone. Focused entirely on your own plate and experience.
Voice: Mention that others were there too — what they got, how it went for them.
Voice: Describe how things looked before you say anything about how they tasted.
Voice: Lead with smell — what hit you first before you even tasted anything.
Voice: Caught one very specific, small detail that others might miss. That is the anchor.
Voice: Do not get into specifics. Say how the whole thing felt overall.
Voice: Do not say whether others should go. Just say what happened to you.
Voice: Focus on whether you would order the same thing again.
Voice: Conscious of how long things took. Time is a detail, not a complaint.
Voice: Casual about it. Was pretty solid, not bad at all. Nothing intense either way.
Voice: Sound like you thought about this before writing. Measured and considered.
